title: Scale Bench
context: Grade 4, the closing topic, and the one the whole chapter has been protecting. An adult sees a conversion done backwards. What is actually at stake is the difference between an amount and the way an amount is written. A weight printed as two point seven five zero kilograms has three decimal places by this chapter's own counting rule, so its denominator is a thousand. A child who tidies it first gets the same weight over a hundred, which is right about the weight and wrong about the question, and has no way at all of seeing the difference, because the two really are equal.

writeup.why: Turn a decimal back into a fraction by counting the places that are printed, and find out what a zero on the end is doing there.
writeup.look: A kitchen scale at the left with a printing display, a bench of three working steps beside it, and a balance beam under the two rows.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Scale Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the weights converted against the weights this phase puts on the pan, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each fraction is finished and the second fixed at however many this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The scale stands at the left of the working area, its body 340 by 360 at 64,220 with a shallow pan drawn across the top of it, and its display 280 by 86 at 94,500. The display prints a weight exactly as it reads and never tidies it: a zero standing at the end of the number is drawn grey but at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, faded or left off. The bench stands to the right of the scale in three working steps, each 210 by 150, at 440,220, 670,220 and 900,220. Carry brings the printed weight across from the display to the first step along a drawn path, with the number unchanged on the way. The first step drops the point out and lays the digits down as the numerator, with nothing else about them altered and no digit lost. The second step counts the decimal places, lighting each printed digit to the right of the point in turn from the point outwards, a zero on the end included and lit like the rest, and writes the count it reaches. The third step writes the denominator as a one followed by one zero for every counted place, the zeros drawn in one at a time directly under the count so that the two can be matched digit for digit. Tidy first takes the same weight, drops a zero off its end, and runs the whole bench again in a second row of three steps directly below at 440,390, 670,390 and 900,390, so both fractions stand on the stage at once and neither is cleared. The balance beam is drawn under the two rows, 420 by 110 at 440,552, with one fraction hung at each end: it holds dead level, because the two amounts are equal, and it never tips either way at any point. The written form panel stands beside it, 280 by 110 at 870,552, holding the two written forms one above the other with their places counted off, plainly different lengths and never drawn level. The can do list runs along the foot, 1086 by 56 at 64,672, carrying six statements to be ticked against the work standing on the bench. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a numerator or a denominator is asked for, with a fraction key beside them that draws a bar and opens a box above and a box below, and under those a tick key for the can do list, which can only be pressed while the work a statement is about is standing on the bench. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception. A part or a column standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The beam and the panel are two different instruments and they are never drawn agreeing with each other. The beam is about how much, so it is level; the panel is about how it is written, so it is uneven. Nothing on this stage ever rubs a printed digit out, and the tidied row is built beside the printed one rather than over it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the weight the child read, the fraction built from its printed places, and the tidied row standing under it with the beam level between them.

phases.win: the digits settle as the numerator with nothing else about them changed
phases.does: carries the weight to the bench and drops the point out of it
phases.goal: the numerator is the digits with the point taken out and nothing else changed
phases.says: Take the dot out and leave the digits alone. What have you got?
phases.check: Away from the screen: read a weight off a scale and write its numerator. Did every digit make it across?
phases.feels: the point comes out and the digits stay exactly as they were, in the same order and all of them
phases.hands: Put a packet on a kitchen scale and let the class read the display out exactly as it stands, including anything on the end. Write the digits down without the point and check that the same digits are there, in the same order, with none lost. Then cover the point on the written number with a finger and ask what is left, and whether anything else has been changed.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many digits are on the display? Second rung, the phase's: how many are in your numerator? Third rung: the bench is cut to a weight with two digits and the child carries it across. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the number came off the display with the point in it and taking a mark out of a number feels like changing the number, which is the one thing the step says not to do.
wrong.move: keeps the point in the numerator, so the top of the fraction is still a decimal.
wrong.screen: the point is lifted out of the number along a drawn path and set down beside the bench, where it stays visible, and the digits close up into the numerator with none of them moving out of order. The child's version stays standing in the first step, and both are read out as rows of digits so that the only difference between them can be heard.

wrong.why: the whole number part is the part that looks like a number already, and the digits after the point read as something attached to it rather than as part of it.
wrong.move: writes only the digits from one side of the point, keeping the whole number part and dropping the rest.
wrong.screen: the display is carried across again at walking pace with every digit lighting in turn from the left, and the digits settle into the numerator one at a time with the count of digits written above the row. The child's shorter numerator stays exactly where it was written, and the two rows are stood one above the other with the digits that went missing lit in the display.

phases.screen: a weight standing on the scale display with the first working step empty
phases.soWhat: The numerator is the digits with the point taken out and nothing else changed.
phases.concept: Dropping the point to get the top

phases.win: the denominator settles with its zeros drawn in one at a time under the count
phases.does: counts the decimal places and writes one and that many zeros
phases.goal: the denominator is one followed by a zero for every decimal place
phases.says: Count the places after the dot. Now write one and that many zeros.
phases.check: A weight has three decimal places. What goes underneath, and how many zeros does it have?
phases.feels: the bottom number is built rather than remembered, one zero for each place counted
phases.hands: Work two conversions by hand, one with a weight of one decimal place and one with three, and write the counting and the denominator on two lines directly under one another so the zeros line up with the places. Ask what the denominator would be for a weight with four places, without a scale to read it off, and let the class build it from the count.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places did the counter find? Second rung, the phase's: how many zeros does that ask for? Third rung: the bench is cut to a weight of one decimal place and the child builds its denominator. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: every early figure in the chapter had ten underneath it, and ten has quietly become what the bottom of one of these fractions looks like.
wrong.move: writes ten underneath whatever the number of places, because ten was the first denominator the chapter met.
wrong.screen: the place counter is run again with each printed digit after the point lighting in turn and the count written under the row, and the third step then draws the zeros in one at a time under that count, stopping when they match. The child's denominator stays standing where it was written, and the built one is stood beside it with the count drawn above both.

wrong.why: the count is the number the second step just handed over, and the empty box under the bar is the next place anything gets written.
wrong.move: writes the number of places underneath instead of one followed by that many zeros, so two places give a two.
wrong.screen: the count stays lit in the second step and the third step is walked through slowly: a one is written first, then a zero for each place, each zero landing under the place it belongs to. The child's denominator stays in the row, the built denominator is written beside it, and both fractions are read out with the size of the pieces each one is counting drawn underneath them.

phases.screen: the numerator laid down with the denominator slot empty under it
phases.soWhat: The denominator is one followed by a zero for every decimal place.
phases.concept: Building the bottom from the places

phases.win: the count takes in the last zero and the denominator comes out one zero longer
phases.does: counts the printed places with that last zero included and builds the denominator from them
phases.goal: a printed zero on the end takes a decimal place of its own
phases.says: There is a zero on the end. Does it take a place or not?
phases.check: A label reads a weight with a zero printed on its end. How many decimal places is that, and what goes underneath?
phases.feels: the zero on the end is not spare, it is standing in a place and the counting reaches it
phases.hands: Let each group weigh three packets and write each weight down exactly as the scale shows it, trailing zeros and all, before anything is converted. Then convert each one, counting the printed places aloud. Ask any group that rubbed a zero off the end what denominator they ended up with, and stand it beside a group that kept it, so both numbers are on the board together.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last digit the display prints? Second rung, the phase's: is it standing in a decimal place? Third rung: the bench is cut to a weight of two printed places ending in a zero and the child counts and builds. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a zero on the end adds nothing to the amount, and tidying a number before working with it is a habit that has been useful everywhere else.
wrong.move: rubs the zero off the end of the weight before counting, because it looks as though it is doing nothing.
wrong.screen: the weight is carried back to the display and read again exactly as the scale printed it, with the last zero drawn at full strength and lit like every other digit, and the place counter runs from the point outwards taking it in. The child's shorter count stays written under the bench and both counts are left standing, with the denominator built again a zero at a time under the longer one.

wrong.why: the count and the bottom number are written in two different steps, so a count that has been corrected does not automatically reach the number underneath.
wrong.move: counts the printed zero as a place but leaves the denominator the length it would have been without it.
wrong.screen: the count and the denominator are drawn one directly above the other with each zero lined up under the place it stands for, and the last place is left with nothing under it and held lit. The child's denominator stays exactly where it was written, the missing zero is walked into the row under the lit place, and both denominators are read out with the size of their pieces drawn underneath.

phases.screen: a weight with a zero on its end, lit on the display
phases.soWhat: A trailing zero takes a decimal place of its own, so the denominator comes out one zero longer.
phases.concept: A zero on the end still counts

phases.win: the beam holds level while the two written forms stand plainly different beside it
phases.does: runs the tidy first control and reads the two fractions and the beam together
phases.goal: the tidied number gives the same amount and a different written answer
phases.says: Tidy it first and run it again. Same amount? Same writing?
phases.check: A height is printed with two decimal places, the last of them a zero. Write the fraction the question asks for, and say what a child who tidied it first would have written instead.
phases.feels: the beam will not move, and the two written answers are still not the same answer
phases.hands: Weigh one packet and write its weight twice, once exactly as the scale printed it and once tidied, then convert both. Ask the class two questions in this order and never only one of them. Is it the same amount? Yes, and the beam holds level. Is it the same writing? No, and the writing is what the question asked for. Finish on the reverse case: an amount given as seventy hundredths asks for two decimal places, and writing only one of them throws away the very place the words named.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places are printed on this one? Second rung, the phase's: how many are printed on the tidied one? Third rung: the bench is cut to a weight of two printed places and the child runs both rows and reads the beam. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: two different fractions written under one weight look like a contradiction, and rubbing one out is what has always been done with a working that turned out to disagree with another.
wrong.move: decides the two answers cannot both be right and rubs one of them out.
wrong.screen: nothing is rubbed out. Both fractions swing down on to the beam, one at each end, and the beam holds dead level and stays level, while the panel beside it writes the two forms one above the other with their places counted off and their lengths plainly different. Both rows of the bench stay standing above them for as long as anybody wants to look.

wrong.why: tidying has been the right move in every chapter up to this one, and a shorter number is easier to work with and looks better written down.
wrong.move: tidies every weight in sight before converting it, as a habit, including an amount that was given in words as seventy hundredths.
wrong.screen: the words are laid out along the bench with the last word lit, the two places that word asks for are drawn empty to the right of a point, and the child's tidied answer is walked into them, where it reaches only the place nearest the point and leaves the far one open. The beam still holds level under the two amounts, the panel still stands the two written forms apart, and both answers stay on the stage with the place that was thrown away left lit.

phases.screen: both rows on the bench, the printed one above and the tidied one below it
phases.soWhat: A trailing zero leaves the amount alone and takes a decimal place, so it changes the denominator and not the weight.
phases.concept: The right amount can still be the wrong answer

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when tidy first is pressed. The weight lifts off the display a second time, sheds the zero from its end on the way across, and runs the three steps of the lower row on its own: the point drops out, the places count themselves one short of the row above, and the denominator is built a zero at a time under the shorter count. Then both fractions swing down on to the beam, one at each end, and the beam holds absolutely level and stays there, while beside it the panel writes the two forms one above the other with their places counted off and their lengths plainly different. Nothing tips, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a weight stands on the display and the first working step of the bench is empty, with the point still in the number. On the second the numerator is already laid down and the denominator slot under it stands empty with its count unmade. On the third the display carries a weight whose last printed digit is a zero, drawn at full strength and lit, with the place counter waiting. On the fourth both rows of the bench stand one above the other, the printed row worked and the tidied row empty, with the beam drawn level and unloaded beneath them. The running count at the top left holds the weights converted against the weights this phase puts on the pan, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the point in the display, or the empty denominator slot, or the last printed digit, or the unloaded beam, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the display actually says. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any weight on the scale, with as many zeros on the end as the display will carry, the tidied row and the balance beam open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on dropping the point, building the denominator from the places, counting a printed zero on the end, and what tidying a number first costs.
voiceLines: Read the display exactly as it stands, last zero and all.
Take the dot out and leave the digits alone. What have you got?
Count the places after the dot. Now write one and that many zeros.
There is a zero on the end. Does it take a place or not?
Tidy it first and run it again. Same amount? Same writing?
Another weight on the pan. Read it off the way the scale wrote it.
Free play. Any weight on the pan, tidied row and balance beam open.
Carry it back to the scale and count the printed places again, every one of them.
Every weight read as printed, and a level beam under two written answers that are not the same.

observations.why: Taking the point out is the only thing the first step does, so no digit can go missing in it.
observations.soWhat: If a digit disappears between the display and the numerator, the mistake was made in the first step.
observations.observe: The numerator was the digits of the display with the point taken out, and nothing else about them changed.

observations.why: There is one zero for each decimal place, so the two rows can be matched against each other digit for digit.
observations.soWhat: The denominator is built from the count, so a wrong count and a wrong denominator are one mistake and not two.
observations.observe: The zeros of the denominator were drawn in one at a time under the count of places.

observations.why: It is standing in a decimal place, and the count is of the places that are printed rather than of the places a tidy hand would have written.
observations.soWhat: A trailing zero takes a decimal place of its own, so it makes the denominator one zero longer.
observations.observe: The zero printed at the end of the weight lit in the counting like every other digit.

observations.why: The two fractions are the same amount of flour and are not the same piece of writing, and the two instruments measure different things.
observations.soWhat: Two answers can be equal in amount and still be different answers, and a question can be about the writing.
observations.observe: The beam held dead level while the panel beside it stood the two written forms plainly apart.

source_tool.description: A kitchen scale stands at the left of the stage with a pan on it and a display that prints a weight exactly as it reads, any zero on the end included and drawn at full strength. A carry control brings the printed weight across to a bench laid out in three working steps. The first step drops the point out and lays the digits down as the numerator, with nothing else changed. The second counts the decimal places, and it counts what is printed on the display rather than what a tidy hand would have written: a zero on the end is counted, lit, and never dimmed. The third writes the denominator as a one followed by one zero for every counted place, the zeros drawn in one at a time under the count so that the two can be matched. A tidy first control is the one that does the teaching. It takes the same weight, drops a zero off its end, and runs the whole bench again in a second row directly below, so a child sees two different fractions built from what the scale calls one weight. A balance beam under the two rows holds them level, because the amounts are equal, while a written form panel beside it stands the two written forms plainly apart, because they are not the same writing. A can do list along the foot carries six statements to be ticked against the work standing on the bench.
source_tool.art_direction: A kitchen scale and a working bench / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip that can be cut, a ten by ten grid whose cells can be tapped, digit cards that can be picked up, a point card of its own, a ruled place chart with a heading over every column, a kitchen scale with a printing display, and a balance beam.

A whole is always drawn split into parts of the same size, with the parts touching so that the whole is still one thing. Exactly the stated number of parts is drawn, exactly the stated number of them is shaded, and no part overlaps another.

A decimal is always drawn with its point standing clearly between the two parts and never floating above or below the line. Where the two parts are named, the whole number part is named on the left and the decimal part on the right.

A place chart always carries a named heading over every column, holds one digit to a column, and keeps a column of its own for the dot between the ones and the tenths. A bare row of digits with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.

A zero filling an empty decimal place is drawn arriving from the point outwards, on the left of the digits already there, with a short arrow running inward from the point. That arrow never runs the other way.

A zero printed on the end of a decimal is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, tidied away or quietly dropped. The whole teaching of the closing topic is that it counts.

Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one above the other, with whatever measures the difference between them drawn in between. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A column, a place or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a part or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. A digit to the left of the point is deep blue and a digit to the right of it is green, with the decimal point itself vermilion between them in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose and one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and those three hold from the strip to the grid to the chart. A zero holding a place open is grey, whether it was filled in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement, because it is the one digit here doing a job rather than counting something. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. All of that holds in greyscale, because a filling zero is told apart by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a printed zero on the end by the place counter that lights it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

placement.where: At the end, once both conversions have been worked by hand, and with a real scale on the table if there is one. The tool is what keeps the printed number and the tidied one on the stage at the same time, which paper can only do by writing a wrong answer out in full and leaving it.

answer_key.rule: To turn a decimal into a fraction, write the digits without the point and that is the numerator. Count the decimal places. Write one followed by that many zeros underneath. The count is of the places that are PRINTED, not of the places a tidy answer would have had. A weight printed as 2.750 has three decimal places, so it becomes 2750/1000. Tidying it to 2.75 first gives 275/100, which is the same weight and not the number the question was about. A trailing zero changes the written form and leaves the value alone, and this chapter is asking about the written form.
answer_key.wrong: The weight is carried back to the scale and read off the display again, the printed places are counted and lit one at a time with any zero on the end included, and the denominator is built a zero at a time under the count. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Take the point out of 6.3 and the digits left standing are 63, which is the numerator.
One digit sits after the point, so there is one decimal place.
One decimal place gives one followed by one zero underneath, which is ten, so 6.3 is 63/10.
items.answer: 63/10, and the top number is the digits with the point taken out
items.question: Write 6.3 as a fraction, and say where the top number came from.
items.checkpoint: The numerator is the digits with the point removed and nothing else changed.
items.misconception: Dropping a digit along with the point, or writing the whole number part on its own.

steps: Taking the point out leaves 4528, and that is the numerator.
Two digits sit after the point, so there are two decimal places.
Two places give one followed by two zeros, which is a hundred, so 45.28 is 4528/100.
items.question: Write 45.28 as a fraction.
items.checkpoint: One zero underneath for every decimal place, counted after the point.
items.misconception: Writing ten underneath whatever the number of places, because ten was the first denominator met.

steps: The display prints three digits after the point, and the last of the three is a zero.
A printed zero takes a place just as any other digit does, so there are three decimal places.
Taking the point out gives 1450, and three places give a thousand underneath, so the fraction is 1450/1000.
items.question: A scale prints a weight as 1.450 kg. How many decimal places is that, and what fraction does it give?
items.checkpoint: A trailing zero takes a decimal place and so changes the denominator.
items.misconception: Rubbing the last zero out before counting, because it looks as though it is doing nothing.

steps: Tidying to 1.45 leaves two decimal places, so the conversion gives 145/100.
That is the same weight: 145/100 and 1450/1000 sit level on the beam and neither is heavier.
But the question was about the number as it was printed, which has three places, so the answer asked for is 1450/1000.
items.answer: They write 145/100, which is the same weight and not the number that was printed
items.question: A child tidies that same 1.450 kg to 1.45 and then converts it. What do they write, and why is it not the answer that was asked for?
items.checkpoint: A trailing zero leaves the amount alone and takes a decimal place, so it changes the denominator and not the weight.
items.misconception: Believing the two answers cannot both be right, when they are equal in amount and different in written form.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: In turning 15.7 into a fraction, what is the numerator, and where does it come from?
items.final_answer: 157, which is the digits with the point taken out

items.question: Write 7.209 as a fraction, and say how the denominator was chosen.
items.final_answer: 7209/1000, because three decimal places give one followed by three zeros

items.question: A label reads 2.60 m. Write it as a fraction, counting the places that are printed.
Is 4.500 the same amount as 4.5, and is it the same written form?
items.final_answer: The same amount, but not the same written form, because 4.500 has three decimal places and 4.5 has one

items.question: A height is printed as 1.30 m. One child writes 130/100 and another tidies it to 1.3 and writes 13/10. Which one answered the question that was asked?
items.final_answer: The first one, because the printed number has two decimal places; the two are the same height, but 130/100 is the written form the question was about

items.question: A bag is printed as 5.250 kg. Write it as a fraction, and say what a child who tidied it first would have written instead.
items.final_answer: 5250/1000, and a child who tidied to 5.25 first would have written 525/100, the same weight in a different written form

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: prints a weight exactly as it reads, any zero on the end included
lays the digits down without the point as the numerator
counts the printed decimal places and lights each one, zeros included
writes one and then a zero for every counted place
drops a zero off the end and runs the whole bench again in a second row
holds the two amounts level, because they are equal
stands the two written forms side by side, because they are not the same
carries six statements to be ticked against the work standing on the bench

teaching_notes: Bring a kitchen scale if there is one, and let the class read the display exactly as it stands. The chapter's own worked example turns nine point two into 92/10, and that is the easy half of this topic. The hard half is the shopping question, where a weight is printed as two point seven five zero kilograms and becomes 2750/1000 because three decimal places are printed. Say it as two separate questions and ask them in that order. Is it the same amount? Yes, and the beam holds level. Is it the same writing? No, and the writing is what was asked for. A class that only ever hears the first question will tidy every number in sight, and a class that only ever hears the second will decide that the two weights are different, which is worse. Ask both, every time. The closing self assessment is six statements long, and it is worth running against the bench rather than in the abstract: a child who has built both rows can point at the work that answers each line. The same trap runs the other way earlier in the chapter, where an amount given as seventy hundredths wants two decimal places written out, and writing only one of them throws away the very place the question named.
generation_prompt: Build a converting bench on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A kitchen scale stands at the left of the working area with a pan and a display that prints a weight exactly as it reads, including any zero on the end, which is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed or dropped. A carry control brings the printed weight across to a bench laid out in three working steps. The first step drops the point out and lays the digits down as the numerator, with nothing else changed. The second counts the decimal places, lighting each printed digit after the point in turn, a zero on the end included. The third writes the denominator as a one followed by one zero for every counted place, the zeros drawn in one at a time under the count so the two can be matched. A tidy first control takes the same weight, removes a zero from its end, and runs the whole bench again in a second row directly below, so both fractions stand on the stage together. A balance beam drawn under the two rows holds them level, because the two amounts are equal, while a written form panel beside it stands the two written forms apart, because they are not the same writing. Neither row is marked and neither is cleared. A can do list along the foot of the stage carries six statements for a child to tick against the work standing on the bench. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the number exactly as it is printed. Take the dot out to get the top number. Count the places after the dot, and count any zero on the end too. Write one and that many zeros underneath.
